title: "Compound disturbance, additively modelled"

  - name: Seamus Murphy

abstract: >
  Compound disturbance is routinely described as an interaction and routinely modelled as a sum.
  This study separates the two claims over a mountain pine beetle outbreak and the mixed-severity
  wildfire that followed it in the southern Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia, asking first
  whether the two agents are associated on the ground and second whether their effects on conifer
  regeneration multiply or merely add. The first result concerns the data rather than the forest.
  The annual beetle classifications from which every beetle surface in the parent study descends
  were clipped to the fire perimeter before any classification was run, so they carry nodata across
  almost all of the surrounding unburned forest, and the published red-attack surface is confined
  more tightly still. Read at face value they imply almost no beetle mortality around the fire. The
  provincial Aerial Overview Survey, an independent record that was never clipped, reports attack
  outside the perimeter at a rate no lower than inside it, so any burned against unburned contrast
  measures the clip. What survives is the gradient within the perimeter, where every severity class
  is equally exposed, and there three records sharing no common measurement pathway agree that
  attack peaks at moderate severity; conditioned on lodgepole cover and elevation that peak
  attenuates by about two fifths and still clears a spatial block bootstrap interval at every block
  size the extent can populate, while the fall at high severity is never supported. The second
  result is the general one. Refitting the parent study's point process model with the beetle by
  fire product term returns an emphatic interaction under the Poisson likelihood that model is
  fitted with, and no interaction at all under inference that accounts for the clustering the same
  study documents in its own figures. The coefficients are identical; the intervals differ by a
  factor of two to eight. Compound-disturbance interactions can be reported with a confidence that
  comes from the likelihood rather than from the data.

F_CRUDE <- y ~ sev

# Introduction

Mountain pine beetle outbreak and wildfire increasingly overlap in the conifer forests of western North America, and the overlap is usually described in the language of interaction. Whether the description is earned is a separate question from whether it is common. @talucci2019dead and @meigs2011 both frame the beetle to fire sequence as a modification of fuels and therefore of subsequent severity, and @krawchuk2020 place compound disturbance at the centre of the refugia concept. The claim that the agents interact is, in each case, a claim about a product rather than a sum.

The parent study for this analysis [@murphy2026] modelled conifer regeneration across three four-hectare plots inside the 2015 Mt Midgeley burn, using classified Landsat surfaces for burn severity and for red-stage beetle mortality. Its abstract describes the additive effects of increasing beetle to fire disturbance interactions. Its model, however, enters red attack, grey attack and burn severity as additive main effects with no product term among them. The two statements are not the same statement, and the ambiguity was noticed at the time without being resolved.

This study asks the two questions that separation implies.

The first is whether prior beetle mortality is associated with subsequent burn severity in this landscape. The outbreak ran from 2005 to 2014 and the fire burned in 2015, so the causal arrow runs one way only, from beetle to fire, and never the reverse. The literature on the question is contested rather than empty, so what novelty there is rests on the particular landscape and on the treatment of confounding rather than on the question being new.

The second is whether beetle and fire act additively on regeneration or interact. Here the test is direct: refit the published point process model with the beetle by fire product term and compare it against the published additive fit.

The first question turned out to require a prior question, which is whether the surfaces that would answer it can answer it. @sec-provenance reports that check. It is negative, it is decisive, and it changes the shape of question one before any ecology is attempted.

The second question turned out to require a prior question too, and a less obvious one: not whether the data can support a product term, but whether the likelihood used to fit it can be trusted to say. @sec-interaction reports that the product term is emphatic under the likelihood the parent study fits and absent under inference that accounts for the clustering the parent study itself documents. The coefficients are the same either way. That gap, rather than either question's ecology, is what this paper carries beyond the landscape it was measured in.

# Materials

## Study area and disturbance history {#sec-area}

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the southern Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. A mountain pine beetle outbreak affected the property through the decade to 2014, and the Mt Midgeley wildfire burned part of it in 2015, producing a mixed-severity mosaic. The beetle to fire interval across the burned area ranges from one to eleven years with a median of seven [@murphy2026].

## Local classified surfaces {#sec-local}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-footprints
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Footprints of the local classified surfaces against the terrain grid. Every disturbance surface is confined to a rectangle of roughly eight square kilometres; the terrain grid covers thirty-four times that area."

G   <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Elevation.utm.tif"))
red <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif"))
sev  <- rast(dpath("fire_severity",  "Fire.Severity.NDBR.tif"))
grey <- rast(file.path(GREY_FIX, "rasters", "mpb_grey_corrected.tif"))
per  <- project(vect(dpath("fire_perimiter", "Fire.Perimiter.shp")), crs(G))

footprint <- function(nm, r) {
  e <- as.vector(ext(r))
  w <- e[2] - e[1]; h <- e[4] - e[3]
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         Rows = nrow(r), Cols = ncol(r),
         `Cell (m)` = round(res(r)[1], 2),
         `Width (km)` = round(w / 1000, 2),
         `Height (km)` = round(h / 1000, 2),
         `Extent (km2)` = round(w * h / 1e6, 2))
}

RES_M <- res(red)[1]

FOOT <- bind_rows(
  footprint("Elevation, terrain grid", G),
  footprint("Beetle red stage",        red),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, corrected", grey),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, deprecated", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.GreyStage.tif"))),
  footprint("Beetle continuous (spatstat)", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "MPB.classified.spatstat.tif"))),
  footprint("Burn severity, classified", sev),
  footprint("Beetle by fire intersection", rast(dpath("beetle_fire_interactive", "mpbred_firehigh.tif"))))

PERIM_KM2 <- as.numeric(sum(expanse(per, unit = "km")))
RECT_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Beetle red stage"]
GRID_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Elevation, terrain grid"]

show(FOOT, "tbl-footprints", "lrrrrrr")
```

The fire perimeter encloses `r round(PERIM_KM2, 2)` km^2^. The beetle red-stage raster spans a rectangle of `r RECT_KM2` km^2^ around it, so the raster carries roughly `r round(RECT_KM2 - PERIM_KM2, 2)` km^2^ of ground outside the burn on which beetle attack could in principle have been mapped. The terrain grid covers `r round(GRID_KM2, 0)` km^2^ of the same landscape and shows what surrounds the burn.

## The severity classes, decoded {#sec-decode}

The classified severity raster carries integer codes that are not ordered by severity, and the ordering matters to every table that follows. It is established here from the three binary class masks rather than assumed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-decode
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Decoding the classified burn severity raster against its own binary class masks, and against the fire perimeter. The integer codes are not in severity order. Code 16 falls inside the perimeter but in none of the three severity classes."

P <- rasterize(per, sev, background = 0)

sv <- vals(sev); pv <- vals(P)

## Fraction of a code's cells that fall inside the perimeter. Written once and
## used for both the classification test and the reported percentage.
inside_frac <- function(k) mean(pv[sv == k] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)

## Keyed by class label, valued by the filename token, so the label comes from
## the map rather than from a positional fixup the assertion would then be
## checking against its own input.
MASK_FILE <- c(High = "High", Moderate = "Med", Low = "Low")
DEC <- lapply(names(MASK_FILE), function(cl) {
  hit <- vals(rast(dpath("fire_severity", paste0("Fire.", MASK_FILE[[cl]], ".NDBR.tif")))) == 1
  tibble(Class = cl, Code = unique(sv[hit]), Cells = sum(hit, na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows()

## the two codes that no class mask claims
unclaimed <- setdiff(na.omit(unique(sv)), DEC$Code)
UNC <- tibble(
  Class = ifelse(sapply(unclaimed, inside_frac) > 0.5,
                 "Inside perimeter, unclassified", "Outside perimeter"),
  Code  = unclaimed,
  Cells = sapply(unclaimed, function(k) sum(sv == k, na.rm = TRUE)))

DECODE <- bind_rows(UNC, DEC) |>
  mutate(`Inside perimeter (%)` = round(100 * sapply(Code, inside_frac), 1)) |>
  arrange(match(Class, ROW_ORDER))

## The mapping is load-bearing. Assert it rather than trusting the read.
stopifnot(DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "High"] == 1,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Low"] == 32,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Moderate"] == 34)
CODE_OF <- setNames(DECODE$Code, DECODE$Class)

## Code to label, the inverse of CODE_OF, written once.
sev_label <- function(v) names(CODE_OF)[match(v, CODE_OF)]

show(DECODE, "tbl-decode", "lrrr")
```

Code 1 is high severity and code 34 is moderate, so a table built on the numeric order of the codes would report the two most severe classes the wrong way round. Code 16 is the class that no severity mask claims: `r format(DECODE$Cells[DECODE$Class == "Inside perimeter, unclassified"], big.mark = ",")` cells lying inside the fire perimeter but assigned to none of high, moderate or low.

## The independent record {#sec-aos}

The provincial Aerial Overview Survey is the operational record of forest health in British Columbia. Observers sketch-map damage annually from fixed-wing aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species [@bcaos2026]. It is coarse, it is observer data, and its errors are positional and perceptual rather than spectral. That last property is what makes it useful here: whatever is wrong with it is uncorrelated with the Landsat classification whose footprint is under test.

```{r}
#| label: aos
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Read with an extent filter built in BC Albers; the provincial layer is
## memory-hostile whole. Project after filtering, never before.
e3005 <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005")
aos   <- vect(AOS_GDB, layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = ext(e3005))
AOS_ALL <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM" & aos$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]
AOS_N <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- project(aos, crs(G))
```

Over the terrain grid the survey holds `r format(AOS_ALL, big.mark = ",")` damage polygons of all agents and years, of which `r AOS_N` are mountain pine beetle within the `r min(OUTBREAK)` to `r max(OUTBREAK)` outbreak window used here.

# The provenance of the beetle layers {#sec-provenance}

The scoping for this study reported a contingency table in which beetle red attack rose from near
zero in unburned forest to roughly a fifth of cells at moderate burn severity. Taken at face value
that is a strong compound-disturbance signal. It is also exactly the pattern a clipped raster would
manufacture, and the clip is the first thing to rule out.

## Where the beetle rasters stop {#sec-perimeter}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-perimeter
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Where each beetle surface stops, against the fire perimeter, on the native beetle grid. The annual rasters carry nodata over almost the whole area outside the perimeter, and the two derived surfaces inherit it."

Pr <- rasterize(per, red, background = 0)
INPER <- vals(Pr) == 1
CELLS_OUT <- sum(!INPER)

## What counts as attack on each surface, named once. Written out fifteen times
## between them before this existed, which is fifteen places to edit if the grey
## encoding ever gains a second nonzero code.
GREY_HIT <- vals(grey) > 0
RED_HIT  <- vals(red) == 1
N_RED    <- sum(RED_HIT)

## A cell is observed if any annual raster in the outbreak window carries data
## there. -128 and 128 are the nodata sentinels these files use alongside NA.
is_obs <- function(f) { v <- vals(rast(f)); !(is.na(v) | v == -128 | v == 128) }
OBS <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(ANN, is_obs))

stop_at <- function(nm, present, note) {
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         `Cells present` = sum(present),
         `Inside perimeter` = sum(present & INPER),
         `Outside perimeter` = sum(present & !INPER),
         Note = note)
}

STOPS <- bind_rows(
  stop_at("Annual rasters, any data", OBS, "nodata over the rest"),
  stop_at("Corrected grey stage, 2005 to 2011", GREY_HIT, "union of code 44"),
  stop_at("Red stage, as published", RED_HIT, "substituted for a missing layer"))

## The claim below is that every annual file carries the same nodata footprint,
## so it is counted here rather than recalled.
ND_COUNTS <- vapply(ANN_ALL, function(f) sum(!is_obs(f)), integer(1))
ND_OUT    <- vapply(ANN_ALL, function(f) sum(!is_obs(f) & !INPER), integer(1))
## The prose says every annual file carries the same nodata count. Assert it.
stopifnot(length(unique(ND_COUNTS)) == 1L)

OBS_OUT   <- sum(OBS & !INPER)
GREY_OUT  <- sum(GREY_HIT & !INPER)
RED_OUT   <- sum(RED_HIT & !INPER)
PCT_OBS_OUT <- 100 * OBS_OUT / CELLS_OUT

show(STOPS, "tbl-perimeter", "lrrrl")
```

The annual rasters carry data on `r round(PCT_OBS_OUT, 1)` per cent of the
`r format(CELLS_OUT, big.mark = ",")` cells lying outside the fire perimeter, and nodata on the
rest. Every beetle surface in the study descends from those files, so every one of them inherits the
boundary: the corrected grey union places `r GREY_OUT` of its `r sum(GREY_HIT)` cells
outside the perimeter and the published red-stage surface places `r RED_OUT` of its `r N_RED`.

**The clip is in the source data, not in any downstream step.** All `r length(ANN_ALL)` annual files
carry an identical nodata count of `r format(ND_COUNTS[1], big.mark = ",")` cells,
`r format(ND_OUT[1], big.mark = ",")` of which lie outside the perimeter, and the boundary it traces
is the fire perimeter, which is a shape no property of beetle ecology would produce. Whoever
prepared the time series clipped it to the burn before the classification that used it was ever run.

## Two nested masks, not one {#sec-nested}

The red and grey surfaces do not stop in the same place, and the difference matters.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nested
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The two surfaces against the classified severity footprint. Grey attack is recorded throughout the perimeter; red attack is confined to the three classified severity classes and is absent from the cells inside the perimeter that no class mask claims."

SEV <- resample(sev, red, method = "near")
CLASSIFIED <- vals(SEV) %in% CODE_OF[SEV_LEVELS]

## The three regions are not nested: 22 cells carry a classified severity code
## and fall outside the rasterised perimeter, so these masks are kept as written
## rather than derived from one another by grouping.
REGION <- list(`Outside the fire perimeter`               = !INPER,
               `Inside perimeter, unclassified severity`  = INPER & !CLASSIFIED,
               `Inside the classified severity footprint` = CLASSIFIED)
pct_by_region <- function(v) round(100 * vapply(REGION, function(m) mean(v[m]), numeric(1)), 1)

NEST <- tibble(Region = names(REGION),
               Cells = vapply(REGION, sum, integer(1)),
               `Annual data (%)` = pct_by_region(OBS),
               `Grey attack (%)` = pct_by_region(GREY_HIT),
               `Red attack (%)`  = pct_by_region(RED_HIT))

show(NEST, "tbl-nested", "lrrrr")
```

Inside the perimeter but outside the classified severity footprint, the annual rasters are
`r NEST$"Annual data (%)"[2]` per cent observed and the corrected grey union records attack in
`r NEST$"Grey attack (%)"[2]` per cent of cells. The published red-stage surface records it in
`r NEST$"Red attack (%)"[2]` per cent. That contrast cannot be ecological: the same ground, in the
same years, is either a third attacked or not attacked at all depending on which derivative of the
same annual files is consulted.

So there are two clips, one inside the other. The annual series is clipped to the fire perimeter,
and `Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif` is confined more tightly still, to the ground where burn severity
was classified. The narrower one is an accident of substitution rather than a decision: the layer
the published analysis intended to use, `mpb_red_na.tif`, is missing from the repository, and
`Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif` was put in its place [@murphy2026greyfix].

## The same test against the independent survey {#sec-crosscheck}

If the zeroes are ecological, the provincial survey should also find little beetle attack outside
the burn. If they are clipping, the survey should find as much there as anywhere. The small sliver
of annual data that does extend beyond the perimeter provides a second, internal check on the same
question.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-crosscheck
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The two local surfaces against the independent Aerial Overview Survey, by burn severity class. Local rates are computed only over cells the annual rasters actually observe. The survey finds no shortage of beetle attack outside the burn, and neither does the small observed sliver of the local data."

A  <- rasterize(aos, red, background = 0)
EL <- resample(G, red)

## Class on the perimeter first, then on severity within it. Keying this table on
## the severity code alone would put 67 in-perimeter cells that the severity
## raster codes 0 into the "outside" row and inflate what little the local data
## says out there by a factor of seven.
CC <- tibble(sev = vals(SEV), grey = GREY_HIT, red = RED_HIT, aos = vals(A) == 1,
             elev = vals(EL), obs = OBS, inper = INPER) |>
  mutate(Class = ifelse(!inper, OUTSIDE,
                 ifelse(sev %in% CODE_OF[SEV_LEVELS], sev_label(sev), UNCLASSED))) |>
  group_by(Class) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(),
            `Observed (%)` = round(100 * mean(obs), 1),
            Observed = sum(obs),
            `Grey (%)` = round(100 * mean(grey[obs]), 1),
            `Red (%)`  = round(100 * mean(red[obs]), 1),
            `Survey (%)` = round(100 * mean(aos), 1),
            `Elevation (m)` = round(mean(elev, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(match(Class, ROW_ORDER))

OUTROW <- CC |> filter(Class == OUTSIDE)
BURNED <- CC |> filter(Class %in% SEV_LEVELS)

show(CC, "tbl-crosscheck", "lrrrrrrr") |>
  row_spec(which(CC$Class == OUTSIDE), background = "#f7e7e7")
```

The shaded row carries the argument. Outside the fire perimeter the survey records
`r sprintf("%.1f", OUTROW$"Survey (%)")` per cent of the ground as attacked, a rate no lower than
anything inside the burn and higher than two of the three burned classes. The local surfaces report
nothing there at all, and they report nothing because they see nothing: of
`r format(OUTROW$Cells, big.mark = ",")` cells outside the perimeter the annual rasters observe
`r OUTROW$Observed`.

That figure is worth stating plainly rather than converting to a rate. The local record is not
sparse outside the burn, it is very nearly absent, and `r OUTROW$Observed` cells cannot corroborate
or contradict anything. The comparison therefore rests on the survey alone, which is sufficient: an
independent census of the same ground in the same years finds beetle attack there in ordinary
abundance. The zero the published red-stage surface reports outside the burn is a statement about
the extent of the file, not about the forest.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mask
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The clip, mapped. Top left, the published red-stage surface, which stops at the classified burn. Top right, the corrected grey-stage union, which reaches the fire perimeter and stops there. Bottom left, the burn severity classes. Bottom right, the independent Aerial Overview Survey, which does not stop at anything. The unburned ground in the two upper panels is empty because it was never observed, not because it was never attacked."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 9.6

perim_sf <- st_as_sf(per)

## Relabel each surface from its raw codes so the legends carry meaning rather
## than integers. Cells shown white are outside the fire perimeter entirely.
relabel <- function(r, from, to) {
  out <- r
  values(out) <- factor(to[match(vals(r), from)], levels = to)
  out
}
panel <- function(r, title, pal) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    geom_sf(data = perim_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey15", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal, na.value = "white", name = NULL,
                      na.translate = FALSE, drop = FALSE) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
    labs(title = title) +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9, hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(9, "pt"),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
          legend.margin = margin(t = 2, b = 0))
}

## relabel() maps anything outside `from` to NA, and the outside-perimeter code
## is not in SEV_ORDER, so those cells already render as na.value white. Masking
## them by hand first was doing the same work twice.
SEV_ORDER <- c(UNCLASSED, SEV_LEVELS)
sev_lab <- relabel(SEV, CODE_OF[SEV_ORDER], SEV_ORDER)

## Unobserved cells are shown as a class of their own rather than as absence.
beetle_panel <- function(r, title, col) {
  x <- r
  values(x) <- factor(ifelse(!OBS, "Not observed",
                      ifelse(vals(r) > 0, "Attack", "No attack")),
                      levels = c("Not observed", "No attack", "Attack"))
  panel(x, title, c(`Not observed` = "white", `No attack` = "grey88", Attack = col))
}

p1 <- beetle_panel(red,  "Red stage, as published", "#b2182b")
p2 <- beetle_panel(grey, "Grey stage, corrected 2026-06-02", "#7b3294")
p3 <- panel(sev_lab, "Burn severity classes",
            setNames(c("grey70", "#fddbc7", "#ef8a62", "#67001f"), SEV_ORDER))
p4 <- panel(relabel(A, c(0, 1), c("Not attacked", "Beetle attack")),
            "Aerial Overview Survey, beetle",
            c(`Not attacked` = "grey88", `Beetle attack` = "#2166ac"))

## Rendered once. Printing FIG_MASK as well would draw the same four panels a
## second time on knitr's device; the chunk's fig-width, fig-height and dpi
## already match these arguments, so the embedded image is identical.
FIG_MASK <- (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
FIG_PATH <- file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-mask.png")
ggsave(FIG_PATH, FIG_MASK, width = 9, height = 9.6, dpi = 300)
knitr::include_graphics(FIG_PATH)
```

## What survives {#sec-survives}

The clip destroys any comparison that crosses the fire perimeter and leaves untouched any comparison
made entirely inside it. The three severity classes all sit within the perimeter and are observed at
better than `r floor(min(BURNED$"Observed (%)"))` per cent, so the clip cannot generate differences
among them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-withinburn
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Beetle attack across burn severity within the fire perimeter, in the two local surfaces and in the independent survey. All three peak at moderate severity and fall at high."

WB <- BURNED |>
  select(Class, Cells, `Grey (%)`, `Red (%)`, `Survey (%)`, `Elevation (m)`) |>
  arrange(match(Class, SEV_LEVELS))
shape <- function(col) paste(sprintf("%.1f", WB[[col]]), collapse = ", ")
PEAKS <- vapply(c("Grey (%)", "Red (%)", "Survey (%)"),
                function(k) WB$Class[which.max(WB[[k]])], character(1))
stopifnot(length(unique(PEAKS)) == 1L)
show(WB, "tbl-withinburn", "lrrrrr")
```

Three records agree on the shape. The corrected grey union runs `r shape("Grey (%)")` per cent
across low, moderate and high severity, the published red-stage surface `r shape("Red (%)")`, and
the independent survey `r shape("Survey (%)")`. All three peak at `r tolower(unique(PEAKS))` and
fall at high, and the assertion above fails the render if they ever stop agreeing. The two local
surfaces share a measurement pathway with each other but not with the survey, so the agreement is
not one instrument repeating itself.

That agreement is not yet evidence about fire. The elevation column is the reason. Moderate severity
occupies the highest mean elevation of the three burned classes at
`r WB$"Elevation (m)"[WB$Class == "Moderate"]` m, and the companion refugia analysis of this
landscape finds beetle attack peaking near 1,430 m for reasons that have nothing to do with fire
[@murphy2026refugia]. A severity gradient that is also an elevation gradient will reproduce the
beetle elevation optimum whether or not severity matters. Conditioning on host abundance and on
elevation is therefore the first task of the next phase, not a robustness check appended to it.

# Does the gradient survive conditioning? {#sec-conditioning}

Three records agreeing that attack peaks at moderate severity is not yet evidence that severity is
doing the work. Both agents track host abundance and topography, and lodgepole-rich, mid-elevation
stands are both more attackable and more burnable, so an apparent association between them may be
host distribution seen twice. This section conditions on both.

## The analysis frame and the host layer {#sec-frame}

```{r}
#| label: frame
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Host comes from the provincial inventory, shared with the companion refugia
## study; see 02.inputs/vri/README.md. Lodgepole cover is summed across the three
## species slots because a polygon can carry it in any of them.
vri <- project(vect(VRI_PATH), crs(red))
pl_pct <- function(cd, pct) ifelse(!is.na(cd) & grepl("^PL", cd),
                                   ifelse(is.na(pct), 0, pct), 0)
vri$PL_PCT <- pl_pct(vri$SPECIES_CD_1, vri$SPECIES_PCT_1) +
              pl_pct(vri$SPECIES_CD_2, vri$SPECIES_PCT_2) +
              pl_pct(vri$SPECIES_CD_3, vri$SPECIES_PCT_3)

## The frame is every observed cell inside the fire perimeter. The response is the
## corrected grey union, which is the denser of the two local surfaces and the
## only one observed throughout the perimeter.
RC <- rowColFromCell(red, seq_len(ncell(red)))

FR <- tibble(y    = as.integer(GREY_HIT),
             sev  = sev_label(vals(SEV)),
             elev = vals(EL),
             pl   = vals(rasterize(vri, red, field = "PL_PCT")),
             row  = RC[, 1],
             col  = RC[, 2]) |>
  filter(INPER, OBS, !is.na(elev), !is.na(pl)) |>
  mutate(sev  = factor(ifelse(sev == UNCLASSED, "Unclassified", sev),
                       levels = c(SEV_LEVELS, "Unclassified")),
         host = as.integer(pl > 0),
         ec   = (elev - 1400) / 100) |>       # elevation in 100 m, centred
  ## A handful of cells inside the perimeter carry the outside-perimeter severity
  ## code and fall outside the four levels above. Dropping them here is what keeps
  ## model.matrix and the response the same length; without it model.matrix
  ## silently drops the rows and every bootstrap index is off by that many.
  ## This is the only NA filter on sev: an NA present before the mutate stays NA
  ## through it, so filtering earlier as well would be the same rows twice.
  filter(!is.na(sev))

stopifnot(!anyNA(FR$sev), !anyNA(FR$y), !anyNA(FR$elev), !anyNA(FR$pl),
          nrow(model.matrix(F_ADJ, FR)) == nrow(FR),
          nrow(model.matrix(F_QUAD, FR)) == nrow(FR))

N_FR <- nrow(FR); N_HIT <- sum(FR$y)
```

The frame is `r format(N_FR, big.mark = ",")` cells, of which `r format(N_HIT, big.mark = ",")`
carry grey-stage attack. Lodgepole is present on `r round(100 * mean(FR$host))` per cent of them.

## Host and elevation cannot be separated at this extent {#sec-collinear}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-host
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Attack, host cover and elevation by burn severity class, and the crude contrast between stands carrying lodgepole and stands without it."

## One summarise body, two stratifications. The columns differed in nothing.
strat <- function(g) FR |> group_by(Stratum = g) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(), `Attacked (%)` = round(100 * mean(y), 1),
            `Lodgepole (%)` = round(mean(pl), 1),
            `Elevation (m)` = round(mean(elev)), .groups = "drop")

HOST <- bind_rows(strat(paste0(as.character(FR$sev), " severity")),
                  strat(ifelse(FR$host == 1, "Lodgepole present", "Lodgepole absent")))

R_PL_EL <- cor(FR$pl, FR$elev)
H_PRES <- HOST$`Attacked (%)`[HOST$Stratum == "Lodgepole present"]
H_ABS  <- HOST$`Attacked (%)`[HOST$Stratum == "Lodgepole absent"]

## The two frames are built by different paths; assert they still agree on the
## quantity both report, so a divergence cannot become silent.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  WB$`Grey (%)`,
  HOST$`Attacked (%)`[match(paste0(SEV_LEVELS, " severity"), HOST$Stratum)])))

show(HOST, "tbl-host", "lrrrr") |>
  pack_rows("By burn severity", 1, 4) |> pack_rows("By host presence", 5, 6)
```

The crude host contrast is large: `r H_PRES` per cent of cells carrying lodgepole were attacked
against `r H_ABS` per cent of cells without it, the same direction and roughly the same magnitude
the companion study finds at landscape extent. But lodgepole cover and elevation correlate at
`r sprintf("%.2f", R_PL_EL)` across this frame, and that is the difficulty. At landscape extent the
two can be separated because the elevation gradient runs far enough for pine-poor ground to occur
at every height. Inside an eight square kilometre burn it does not.

## The severity gradient, conditioned {#sec-conditioned}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-conditioned
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Burn severity coefficients on grey-stage attack, as log-odds against low severity, crude and then conditioned on host presence and elevation. Intervals are spatial block bootstrap percentiles at 500 m blocks. An interval that excludes zero is marked."

## glm.fit on a prebuilt model matrix rather than formula glm: arithmetically
## identical and roughly thirty times faster over the bootstrap.
bfit <- function(X, y, idx) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(glm.fit(X[idx, , drop = FALSE], y[idx], family = binomial()))
  if (!f$converged) rep(NA_real_, ncol(X)) else f$coefficients
}
blocks_of <- function(side_m) {
  s <- round(side_m / RES_M)
  split(seq_len(nrow(FR)), paste(FR$row %/% s, FR$col %/% s))
}
block_boot <- function(form, side_m = BLOCK_M, seed = 42) {
  X <- model.matrix(form, FR); y <- FR$y
  est <- bfit(X, y, seq_len(nrow(FR)))
  ids <- blocks_of(side_m); K <- length(ids)
  set.seed(seed)
  M <- vapply(seq_len(B_BOOT),
              function(b) bfit(X, y, unlist(ids[sample.int(K, K, TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)),
              numeric(ncol(X)))
  ci <- apply(M, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Term = colnames(X), Estimate = est, Lower = ci[1, ], Upper = ci[2, ], K = K)
}

M_CRUDE <- block_boot(F_CRUDE)
M_ADJ   <- block_boot(F_ADJ)
M_QUAD  <- block_boot(F_QUAD)

## Interval formatting and the clears-zero verdict, written once. The verdict is
## a logical test on the numbers, never a string compared against a label.
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi) sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", lo, hi)
clears <- function(lo, hi) lo * hi > 0

pick <- function(m, lbl) m |> filter(Term != "(Intercept)") |>
  transmute(Model = lbl, Term,
            Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
            Interval = ci_txt(Lower, Upper),
            ` ` = ifelse(clears(Lower, Upper), "clears zero", ""))
COND <- bind_rows(pick(M_CRUDE, "Severity only"),
                  pick(M_ADJ,   "+ host + elevation"),
                  pick(M_QUAD,  "+ elevation squared"))

gv <- function(m, tm) m$Estimate[m$Term == tm]
MOD_CRUDE <- gv(M_CRUDE, "sevModerate"); MOD_ADJ <- gv(M_ADJ, "sevModerate")
ATTEN <- 100 * (1 - MOD_ADJ / MOD_CRUDE)
show(COND, "tbl-conditioned", "llrll") |> collapse_rows(1, valign = "top")
```

Three things follow, and only the first is a positive result.

**Moderate severity survives conditioning, attenuated.** The crude coefficient of
`r sprintf("%.3f", MOD_CRUDE)` falls to `r sprintf("%.3f", MOD_ADJ)` once host presence and
elevation are in the model, so roughly `r round(ATTEN)` per cent of the crude association is
host and terrain. What remains still clears the block interval. Adding a quadratic elevation term
moves it hardly at all.

**High severity is never distinguishable from low.** Its interval spans zero in every specification.
The non-monotone shape that all three records trace is therefore a claim the data supports at its
peak and not at its fall: attack is elevated at moderate severity, and whether it declines at high
severity cannot be settled from `r format(HOST$Cells[HOST$Stratum == "High severity"], big.mark = ",")`
cells. **Do not report a demonstrated decline at high severity.**

**Host cover cannot be separated from elevation here, and elevation wins.** Entered alongside
elevation, host presence carries an interval that spans zero comfortably, despite the crude contrast
of `r H_PRES` against `r H_ABS` per cent. Elevation is the only covariate whose interval excludes
zero in every specification. This does not contradict the companion study's finding that host
governs the landscape pattern; it means that at this extent the question cannot be asked, because
the two predictors are `r sprintf("%.2f", R_PL_EL)` correlated and the burn is too small to break
the tie.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-elev
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The elevation term inside the burn, against the landscape-scale form the companion study reports. The quadratic term is negligible and its implied optimum falls far outside the elevation range the burn spans, so within this clip the relationship is monotone."

EL_RANGE <- range(FR$elev)
b1 <- gv(M_QUAD, "ec"); b2 <- gv(M_QUAD, "I(ec^2)")
PEAK <- 1400 + 100 * (-b1 / (2 * b2))

## Estimate with its interval, by term. gv() already did the estimate half.
term_ci <- function(m, tm) {
  r <- m[m$Term == tm, ]
  sprintf("%.3f  %s", r$Estimate, ci_txt(r$Lower, r$Upper))
}

ELT <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Elevation range spanned by the burn",
               "Linear elevation, log-odds per 100 m",
               "Quadratic elevation term",
               "Implied optimum of the fitted quadratic",
               "Landscape-scale optimum, companion study"),
  Value = c(sprintf("%.0f to %.0f m", EL_RANGE[1], EL_RANGE[2]),
            term_ci(M_ADJ, "ec"),
            term_ci(M_QUAD, "I(ec^2)"),
            sprintf("%.0f m", PEAK),
            "about 1,430 m"))
show(ELT, "tbl-elev", "ll")
```

The companion study finds beetle attack peaking near 1,430 m across 1,776 m of relief
[@murphy2026refugia]. Inside this burn the fitted optimum lands at `r round(PEAK)` m, far below
anything the clip contains, which is the arithmetic way of saying the quadratic has no support here:
over `r round(diff(EL_RANGE))` m of truncated gradient the relationship is monotone increasing. The
landscape-scale hump is not contradicted, it is invisible. An analyst working only inside this
perimeter would report that beetle attack rises with elevation without limit.

## How much inference this extent supports {#sec-blocks}

Moran's I on the response is high and the residuals stay dependent well beyond a single cell, so
naive standard errors would be meaningless. The block bootstrap fixes that, but the block size is
not free: blocks must be large enough to contain the dependence and numerous enough to resample.
Over a burn this size the two requirements collide.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocks
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The moderate-against-low severity coefficient under block bootstraps of increasing block size, with the number of blocks each affords. The estimate is fixed; only the interval changes. The extent caps the largest usable block, not the conclusion."

## The 500 m run is M_ADJ exactly: same formula, same blocks, same seed, same
## draws. Reusing it saves a redundant 400-replicate bootstrap. Each block_boot
## call seeds itself and draws nothing beforehand, so this cannot perturb the
## RNG stream of any other run.
SWEEP_RAW <- lapply(BLOCK_SWEEP, function(m) {
  fit <- if (m == BLOCK_M) M_ADJ else block_boot(F_ADJ, side_m = m)
  fit |> filter(Term == "sevModerate") |> mutate(`Block side (m)` = m)
}) |> bind_rows()

## Numbers stay numbers. Formatting is a leaf, never an input: the previous
## version formatted these bounds into a string and regex-parsed them back.
SWEEP <- SWEEP_RAW |>
  transmute(`Block side (m)`, Blocks = K, Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
            Interval = ci_txt(Lower, Upper),
            ` ` = ifelse(clears(Lower, Upper), "clears zero", "spans zero"))

## The correlogram that justifies the block sizes tried.
res <- residuals(glm(F_ADJ, binomial, FR), type = "pearson")
set.seed(7); ii <- sample(nrow(FR), 3000)

## dist() enumerates pairs in the same column-major order lower.tri() selects,
## so the two vectors stay aligned. The previous form built four dense 3000 by
## 3000 matrices to read two triangles out of them.
dd <- as.vector(dist(cbind(FR$row[ii], FR$col[ii]))) * RES_M
rr <- outer(res[ii], res[ii], "*") / var(res[ii])
rr <- rr[lower.tri(rr)]
bins <- cut(dd, c(0, 100, 200, 300, 500, 800, 1200, Inf))
CORR <- tibble(`Lag (m)` = levels(bins),
               `Residual correlation` = round(as.numeric(tapply(rr, bins, mean)), 3))

show(SWEEP, "tbl-blocks", "rrrll")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlogram
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Residual correlogram of the conditioned model. Dependence is strong within 100 m and has largely decayed by 500 m, which is the basis for the block sizes tried above."

show(CORR, "tbl-correlogram", "lr")
```

Residual dependence falls from `r CORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` within 100 m to
`r CORR$"Residual correlation"[4]` by 500 m, so a 500 m block contains most of it. The burn spans
about 4.0 by 2.0 km, which affords `r SWEEP$Blocks[SWEEP$"Block side (m)" == BLOCK_M]` blocks at
that size and only `r SWEEP$Blocks[which.max(SWEEP$"Block side (m)")]` at
`r max(SWEEP$"Block side (m)")` m. The companion study uses roughly 1 km blocks over a landscape
that affords hundreds; here 1 km would afford eight, which is not a bootstrap.

```{r}
#| label: sweep-summary
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Let the sweep state its own conclusion rather than asserting one that a
## refit might quietly invalidate.
N_CLEAR  <- sum(clears(SWEEP_RAW$Lower, SWEEP_RAW$Upper))
WEAKEST  <- SWEEP_RAW$`Block side (m)`[which.min(SWEEP_RAW$Lower)]
WEAK_LO  <- min(SWEEP_RAW$Lower)
```

**So the moderate-severity result is reported with its dependence stated.** It clears the interval
at `r N_CLEAR` of the `r nrow(SWEEP)` block sizes tried, which is all of them, so the conclusion
does not rest on a convenient choice of block. It is weakest at `r WEAKEST` m, where the lower bound
sits at `r sprintf("%.3f", WEAK_LO)`, barely above zero on
`r SWEEP$Blocks[SWEEP$"Block side (m)" == WEAKEST]` blocks. That is the honest edge of what this
extent supports, and it is why the sweep is reported rather than a single interval.

The general point is not a robustness check that the study passed. It is the study's own subject
matter arriving in its own inference: the extent that makes the compound-disturbance question
askable at all is the same extent that decides how firmly it can be answered, and an analyst who
reported only the 500 m interval would be concealing that the margin at 750 m is a hair's
breadth.

# Do the two agents interact in the model? {#sec-interaction}

The first question asked whether beetle and fire are associated on the ground. This one asks whether
their effects on what grew back multiply or merely add. It is the question the parent study's title
and abstract assert an answer to and its model never puts to the test, and unlike question A it is
untouched by the perimeter clip, because the seedling point pattern lies wholly inside the burn and
every cell entering the model is equally masked.

The test is direct. Refit the published model with the beetle by fire product term and compare.

## The published model and the frame it is fitted on {#sec-ppframe}

The parent study models conifer regeneration as an inhomogeneous point process over three
four-hectare plots, fitted by the Berman-Turner device: the seedlings enter as data points, a regular
grid of dummy points carries the quadrature weights, and the trend is estimated by weighted Poisson
regression on the pooled set [@baddeley2000]. The specification is reproduced here exactly, including
its quadrature spacing, so that anything that changes when the product term is added is the product
term and not a difference of setup.

```{r}
#| label: ppframe
#| echo: true

PLOTS <- lapply(1:3, function(i)
  st_transform(st_read(dpath(sprintf("plot_locations/Plot%d.shp", i)), quiet = TRUE), 32611))
WIN <- st_union(do.call(rbind, lapply(PLOTS, function(p) p["geometry"])))
WIN_HA <- as.numeric(st_area(WIN)) / 1e4

## The seedling frame. Three counts are in circulation for this point pattern
## and the difference between them is a species filter, not a rival survey, so
## it is derived here rather than chosen.
SEED_ALL <- st_read(dpath("seedlings/Seedlings.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
SPECIES  <- c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "7")   # the seven-species lookup of the parent study
IN_LUT   <- as.character(SEED_ALL$species) %in% SPECIES
SEED     <- SEED_ALL[IN_LUT, ]
N_RAW    <- nrow(SEED_ALL); N_DROP <- sum(!IN_LUT); N_SEED <- nrow(SEED)
## Every retained seedling falls inside the plot windows, so the species filter
## is the whole of the difference between the two counts.
stopifnot(N_RAW - N_DROP == N_SEED,
          all(lengths(st_within(SEED, WIN)) > 0))

## The quadrature grid, at the spacing the published fit used.
bx <- st_bbox(WIN)
GR <- expand.grid(x = seq(bx["xmin"] + PP_DX/2, bx["xmax"], by = PP_DX),
                  y = seq(bx["ymin"] + PP_DX/2, bx["ymax"], by = PP_DX))
GR <- GR[lengths(st_within(st_as_sf(GR, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32611), WIN)) > 0, ]

## The covariates of the published trend, read from the same files it read. The
## grey-stage layer is the corrected union of 2 June 2026, which is the raster
## the parent study's own final refit uses; the legacy layer it replaced is
## discussed in sec-ppsupport.
PP_RAS <- list(
  Aspect = rast(dpath("terrain_environment/Aspect.utm.tif")),
  RIX    = rast(dpath("terrain_environment/Rutm.tif")),
  Wind   = rast(dpath("terrain_environment/Wind.utm.tif")),
  MPB_G  = rast(file.path(GREY_FIX, "rasters", "mpb_grey_corrected.tif")),
  MPB_R  = rast(dpath("beetle_stages/Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif")),
  Fire_H = rast(dpath("fire_severity/Fire.High.NDBR.tif")),
  Fire_L = rast(dpath("fire_severity/Fire.Low.NDBR.tif")),
  Fire_M = rast(dpath("fire_severity/Fire.Med.NDBR.tif")))

PP_BINARY <- c("MPB_G", "MPB_R", "Fire_H", "Fire_L", "Fire_M")
at_points <- function(xy) {
  pt <- vect(as.matrix(xy), type = "points", crs = "EPSG:32611")
  z <- lapply(PP_RAS, function(r) as.numeric(terra::extract(r, project(pt, crs(r)))[, 2]))
  ## Sentinels, as the published script treats them: -1 is flat ground on the
  ## aspect surface and -999 is missing wind. Beers northness on the remainder.
  z$Aspect <- cos(ifelse(z$Aspect == -1, NA, z$Aspect) * pi / 180)
  z$Wind   <- ifelse(z$Wind <= -990, NA, z$Wind)
  for (nm in PP_BINARY) z[[nm]] <- ifelse(is.na(z[[nm]]), NA, as.numeric(z[[nm]] == 1))
  as.data.frame(z)
}

SXY <- st_coordinates(SEED)[, 1:2]
QXY <- as.matrix(GR)
PD <- at_points(SXY); PD$SS_dist <- as.numeric(SEED$distance_m)
PQ <- at_points(QXY)
## Seed source distance is recorded per seedling, not per cell, so the published
## fit carries it to the quadrature points by nearest neighbour. Reproduced here
## because dropping it would change every other coefficient.
PQ$SS_dist <- PD$SS_dist[FNN::get.knnx(SXY, QXY, k = 1)$nn.index[, 1]]

PD$x <- SXY[, 1]; PD$y <- SXY[, 2]; PD$data_pt <- TRUE
PQ$x <- QXY[, 1]; PQ$y <- QXY[, 2]; PQ$data_pt <- FALSE
PP <- rbind(PD, PQ)
## Berman-Turner: quadrature weight is the cell area at a dummy point and a
## negligible constant at a data point, and the response is the reciprocal of
## the weight where a point was observed and zero elsewhere.
PP$w  <- ifelse(PP$data_pt, 1, PP_DX^2)
PP$yy <- ifelse(PP$data_pt, 1 / PP$w, 0)

F_ADD <- yy ~ SS_dist + Aspect + RIX + Wind + MPB_G + MPB_R + Fire_H + Fire_L
F_PROD <- update(F_ADD, . ~ . + MPB_G:Fire_H + MPB_G:Fire_L +
                             MPB_R:Fire_H + MPB_R:Fire_L)
PP <- PP[complete.cases(PP[, all.vars(F_ADD)[-1]]), ]
N_DATA <- sum(PP$data_pt); N_DUMMY <- sum(!PP$data_pt)

## The severity class of each point, needed for the support table and for the
## four-level specification. Built from the class masks, not from the composite
## severity code, which is the encoding trap of sec-decode.
PP$Severity <- factor(
  with(PP, ifelse(Fire_H == 1, "High", ifelse(Fire_M == 1, "Moderate",
         ifelse(Fire_L == 1, "Low", UNCLASSED)))),
  levels = c(SEV_LEVELS, UNCLASSED))
stopifnot(!any(is.na(PP$Severity)))
```

The shapefile holds `r format(N_RAW, big.mark = ",")` points. `r N_DROP` of them carry a species code
outside the seven-species lookup the parent study used, which leaves
`r format(N_SEED, big.mark = ",")`, and every one of those falls inside the plot windows. That
settles a count that has been ambiguous across three documents: the two figures in circulation differ
by a species filter and nothing else, and the third figure, `r format(3886, big.mark = ",")` in the
published abstract, matches neither and is not reproduced by any filter tried here. The fit uses
`r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` data points against `r format(N_DUMMY, big.mark = ",")` quadrature
points over `r sprintf("%.2f", WIN_HA)` ha.

## Reproducing the published fit {#sec-ppreproduce}

Nothing below is worth reading unless the additive fit reproduces. It does, to the precision the
published table is printed at.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppreproduce
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The published additive trend, as reported by the parent study's final refit and as recomputed here from the same rasters. The comparison is the licence for everything that follows: a product term added to a model that did not reproduce would test nothing."

## glm.fit on a prebuilt model matrix, as in sec-conditioned: identical
## arithmetic to formula glm and fast enough to bootstrap.
pfit <- function(X, idx) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(glm.fit(X[idx, , drop = FALSE], PP$yy[idx],
                                weights = PP$w[idx], family = poisson()))
  if (!f$converged) rep(NA_real_, ncol(X)) else f$coefficients
}
X_ADD  <- model.matrix(F_ADD, PP)
X_PROD <- model.matrix(F_PROD, PP)
stopifnot(nrow(X_ADD) == nrow(PP), nrow(X_PROD) == nrow(PP))
B_ADD  <- pfit(X_ADD, seq_len(nrow(PP)))
B_PROD <- pfit(X_PROD, seq_len(nrow(PP)))

PUB <- read.csv(file.path(GREY_FIX, "tables", "Table12_LGCP_coefficients_CORRECTED.csv"))
REPRO <- tibble(Term = names(B_ADD),
                Published = round(PUB$Estimate[match(names(B_ADD), PUB$term)], 4),
                Recomputed = round(unname(B_ADD), 4)) |>
  mutate(Difference = round(Recomputed - Published, 4))
## The reproduction is load-bearing. Fail the render if it ever stops holding.
stopifnot(max(abs(REPRO$Difference)) < 1e-3)
show(REPRO, "tbl-ppreproduce", "lrrr")
```

All `r nrow(REPRO)` coefficients agree, and the assertion above fails the render if they ever stop
agreeing. Two features of the published fit matter for what follows, and both are visible in this
table. The grey-stage coefficient is `r sprintf("%.4f", REPRO$Published[REPRO$Term == "MPB_G"])`,
which is zero to three decimal places: the parent study's own corrected refit already found no
grey-stage main effect. And the two fire terms are indicators for high and low severity, which means
they are contrasts against whatever the reference category contains.

## What each term rests on {#sec-ppsupport}

A coefficient is only as good as the ground that identifies it. Before adding a product term it is
worth counting the quadrature points available to estimate one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppsupport
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Quadrature points inside the three plots, by burn severity class and beetle surface. The published fit's reference category is the union of the two rows that carry no severity indicator, so it pools moderate severity with unburned and unclassified ground."

Q <- PP[!PP$data_pt, ]
sup_row <- function(cls) {
  s <- Q[Q$Severity == cls, ]
  tibble(Class = cls, `Quadrature points` = nrow(s),
         `Area (ha)` = round(nrow(s) * PP_DX^2 / 1e4, 2),
         `Grey attacked` = sum(s$MPB_G == 1),
         `Red attacked`  = sum(s$MPB_R == 1),
         `In reference category` = all(s$Fire_H == 0 & s$Fire_L == 0))
}
SUP <- bind_rows(lapply(levels(PP$Severity), sup_row))
REF_N   <- sum(SUP$`Quadrature points`[SUP$`In reference category`])
REF_MOD <- SUP$`Quadrature points`[SUP$Class == "Moderate"]
GREY_Q  <- sum(Q$MPB_G == 1); RED_Q <- sum(Q$MPB_R == 1)
show(SUP |> mutate(`In reference category` = ifelse(`In reference category`, "yes", "")),
     "tbl-ppsupport", "lrrrrl")
```

Three things follow.

**The reference category is a mixture.** The published fit carries indicators for high and low
severity only, so its reference is every point that is neither, which is
`r format(REF_N, big.mark = ",")` quadrature points, of which `r format(REF_MOD, big.mark = ",")`
are moderate severity and the remainder unburned or unclassified. Moderate is not a neutral baseline
here: it is the class that carries the most beetle attack of the three, as
@tbl-withinburn reports across the whole burn and this table repeats inside the plots. So the
published fire coefficients are contrasts against a pooled category that is
`r round(100 * REF_MOD / REF_N)` per cent the severity class with the strongest beetle association.
Nothing in the published fit is wrong about this, but neither coefficient means what its label
suggests.

**The grey-stage term is now adequately supported, and was not always.** The corrected union carries
grey attack on `r format(GREY_Q, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(nrow(Q), big.mark = ",")` quadrature
points, about `r round(100 * GREY_Q / nrow(Q))` per cent of the plot area. The layer it replaced,
built by a value test the parent study later diagnosed as wrong, carried grey attack on seven
30 m cells in the same plots [@murphy2026greyfix]. A coefficient reported at
p < 10^-10^ in the first submission rested on those seven cells, and the corrected refit moved it to
zero. That correction was made before publication and is to the parent study's credit; it is recorded
here because it is the same failure mode this paper is about, caught one stage earlier.

**Red attack is confined as sec-provenance describes.** It appears on
`r format(RED_Q, big.mark = ",")` quadrature points and on none at all outside the classified
severity classes, which is the narrower of the two clips arriving inside the model.

## The product term {#sec-ppproduct}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppproduct
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The additive trend as published, and the same trend with the four beetle by fire product terms added. Intervals are the naive Poisson intervals the published likelihood implies. On these the interaction is emphatic and three of the four product terms exclude zero."

pois_ci <- function(X, b) {
  eta <- drop(X %*% b); mu <- exp(eta)
  V <- solve(crossprod(X, X * (mu * PP$w)))
  sqrt(diag(V))
}
SE_ADD  <- pois_ci(X_ADD,  B_ADD)
SE_PROD <- pois_ci(X_PROD, B_PROD)

side <- function(b, se, lbl) tibble(
  Term = names(b), Model = lbl, Estimate = round(unname(b), 3),
  Interval = ci_txt(b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se),
  ` ` = ifelse(clears(b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se), "excludes zero", ""))
PRODT <- grep(":", names(B_PROD), value = TRUE)
PROD <- bind_rows(side(B_ADD, SE_ADD, "As published"),
                  side(B_PROD, SE_PROD, "With product terms")) |>
  filter(Term != "(Intercept)")

## The likelihood ratio the published likelihood would report.
dev_of <- function(X, b) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b)) * PP$w; y <- PP$yy * PP$w
  2 * sum(ifelse(y > 0, y * log(y / mu), 0) - (y - mu))
}
LR_STAT <- dev_of(X_ADD, B_ADD) - dev_of(X_PROD, B_PROD)
LR_DF   <- length(PRODT)
LR_P    <- pchisq(LR_STAT, LR_DF, lower.tail = FALSE)
N_PROD_SIG <- sum(clears(B_PROD[PRODT] - 1.96 * SE_PROD[PRODT],
                         B_PROD[PRODT] + 1.96 * SE_PROD[PRODT]))
show(PROD, "tbl-ppproduct", "llrll") |> collapse_rows(2, valign = "top")
```

Read through the likelihood the published model is fitted with, the interaction is not marginal. The
likelihood ratio statistic is `r sprintf("%.1f", LR_STAT)` on `r LR_DF` degrees of freedom, a
p-value below `r format(signif(max(LR_P, 1e-16), 1), scientific = TRUE)`, and
`r N_PROD_SIG` of the `r LR_DF` product terms carry intervals excluding zero. An analyst who stopped
here would report that the compound-disturbance interaction is confirmed, and would have the parent
study's own machinery behind the claim.

Two details ought to give pause before that is written down. The product terms do not share a sign:
grey attack raises regeneration at high severity and lowers it at low severity, and the fitted signs
reverse between the two beetle surfaces on the same severity class. And adding them moves the main
effects sharply, taking the high-severity term from
`r sprintf("%.3f", B_ADD[["Fire_H"]])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", B_PROD[["Fire_H"]])`. A product term
that is real usually leaves the rest of the model roughly where it found it.

## The same terms under inference that respects the clustering {#sec-pphonest}

The published fit's standard errors are Poisson standard errors, which assume that seedlings are
placed independently given the covariates. That assumption is not a background technicality here: the
parent study devotes two figures to rejecting it, reporting inhomogeneous K and L functions with
999-simulation envelopes that show the seedling pattern clustered at every distance examined
[@murphy2026]. A model cannot use a clustered-process figure as a result and an
independent-process likelihood as its inference. The residuals say the same thing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppcorr
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Residual correlogram of the fit with product terms, over the quadrature points. Dependence is strong within one 30 m cell and has decayed by about 100 m, which sets the block sizes tried below."

pres <- function(X, b) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b)) * PP$w
  (PP$yy * PP$w - mu) / sqrt(mu)
}
rq <- pres(X_PROD, B_PROD)[!PP$data_pt]
rq <- rq - mean(rq)
set.seed(7)
jj <- sample(nrow(Q), min(2500L, nrow(Q)))
dd <- as.vector(dist(cbind(Q$x[jj], Q$y[jj])))
rr <- outer(rq[jj], rq[jj]) / mean(rq[jj]^2)
rr <- rr[lower.tri(rr)]
pbins <- cut(dd, c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, Inf))
PCORR <- tibble(`Lag (m)` = levels(pbins),
                `Residual correlation` = round(as.numeric(tapply(rr, pbins, mean)), 3)) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Residual correlation`))
show(PCORR, "tbl-ppcorr", "lr")
```

Dependence runs at `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` inside 25 m and is still
`r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[3]` between 50 and 75 m, crossing zero at around 100 m. A block that
contains it must therefore be at least 75 to 100 m on a side, and a 200 m plot affords few of those.
That collision is the same one @sec-blocks met at landscape scale, arriving again two orders of
magnitude down.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppblocks
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The four product terms and the main effects they modify, under a spatial block bootstrap across block sizes spanning the residual range. The estimates are fixed; only the intervals change. No product term excludes zero at any block size tried."

pp_boot <- function(X, side_m, seed = 11) {
  ids <- split(seq_len(nrow(PP)), paste(PP$x %/% side_m, PP$y %/% side_m))
  K <- length(ids)
  set.seed(seed)
  M <- vapply(seq_len(B_BOOT),
              function(b) pfit(X, unlist(ids[sample.int(K, K, TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)),
              numeric(ncol(X)))
  ci <- apply(M, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Term = colnames(X), Lower = ci[1, ], Upper = ci[2, ], K = K,
         Usable = apply(M, 1, function(v) sum(is.finite(v))))
}

PP_SHOWN <- c("MPB_G", "MPB_R", "Fire_H", "Fire_L", PRODT)
PPB_RAW <- bind_rows(lapply(PP_SWEEP, function(m)
  pp_boot(X_PROD, m) |> filter(Term %in% PP_SHOWN) |> mutate(`Block side (m)` = m)))

PPB <- PPB_RAW |>
  transmute(`Block side (m)`, Blocks = K, Term,
            Estimate = round(B_PROD[Term], 3),
            Interval = ci_txt(Lower, Upper),
            ` ` = ifelse(clears(Lower, Upper), "clears zero", "spans zero"))
show(PPB, "tbl-ppblocks", "rrlrll") |> collapse_rows(1:2, valign = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: pp-verdict
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Let the sweep state the conclusion. Asserting one that a refit could
## invalidate is the error sec-blocks records having made once already.
PROD_ROWS  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(Term %in% PRODT)
PROD_CLEAR <- sum(clears(PROD_ROWS$Lower, PROD_ROWS$Upper))

## Prose reads in words, not in design-matrix column names.
PP_WORDS <- c(MPB_G = "grey-stage attack", MPB_R = "red-stage attack",
              Fire_H = "high burn severity", Fire_L = "low burn severity")
MAIN_KEEP  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(!Term %in% PRODT) |>
  group_by(Term) |> summarise(all_clear = all(clears(Lower, Upper)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(all_clear) |> pull(Term)
MAIN_WORDS <- paste(PP_WORDS[MAIN_KEEP], collapse = " and ")

## The block sizes the correlogram actually licenses, which is not all of the
## sizes tried. Quoting the full sweep's block counts would credit the study with
## the 25 m run's 234 blocks, and a 25 m block does not contain the dependence.
PP_OK    <- PP_SWEEP[PP_SWEEP >= 75]
PP_OK_K  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(`Block side (m)` %in% PP_OK) |>
  distinct(`Block side (m)`, K) |> arrange(desc(K))
PP_OK_TXT <- paste(sprintf("%d at %d m", PP_OK_K$K, PP_OK_K$`Block side (m)`),
                   collapse = " and ")
WIDEN <- PPB_RAW |>
  mutate(naive = 2 * 1.96 * SE_PROD[Term], ratio = (Upper - Lower) / naive) |>
  summarise(lo = min(ratio), hi = max(ratio))
```

**Not one of the `r nrow(PROD_ROWS)` product-term intervals excludes zero.** Across four block sizes
and `r LR_DF` product terms the count that clears is `r PROD_CLEAR`. The estimates have not moved,
because the estimates are not what was wrong; the intervals have widened by a factor of
`r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)` against the naive Poisson intervals of
@tbl-ppproduct, and that factor is the whole of the difference between an interaction that looks
overwhelming and one that is not there.

What survives is thin and worth stating precisely. The only terms among those shown whose intervals
exclude zero at every block size are `r MAIN_WORDS`. Neither is a product term. The regeneration data
support main effects for red-stage beetle attack and low burn severity, and support no statement at
all about the two agents acting together.

This is not a demonstration that the agents do not interact. It is a demonstration that these data
cannot tell. Three plots totalling `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha afford `r PP_OK_TXT` across the
block sizes the residual range permits, and a product term asks the data to resolve a difference of differences across four
severity-by-attack combinations on that footprint. The published likelihood answers the question
confidently because it counts `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings as
`r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` independent pieces of evidence. They are not.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Two questions were asked. Neither returned the answer it was posed to find, and the reasons are
different in kind.

## What the study found {#sec-found}

**Beetle and fire cannot be compared across the fire perimeter in this landscape, because the
surfaces that would do it stop at the perimeter.** The annual classifications from which every local
beetle surface descends carry nodata across almost all of the unburned forest, and they carried it
before any classification that used them was run. The consequence is not a caveat. A contingency
table built across the boundary reports beetle attack rising from a fraction of a per cent in
unburned forest to a fifth at moderate severity, and that table measures the mask. An independent
record that was never clipped, the provincial Aerial Overview Survey, finds attack outside the
perimeter at a rate no lower than inside it.

**Within the burn the severity gradient is real and narrow.** Three records that do not share a
measurement pathway agree that attack peaks at moderate severity, and conditioning on lodgepole cover
and elevation attenuates that peak by about two fifths without removing it. The fall at high severity
is not supported in any specification. So the non-monotone shape is a claim these data carry at its
peak and not at its fall, and the paper reports it that way.

**The beetle by fire interaction is not supported.** Fitted through the likelihood the parent study
uses, it is emphatic: a likelihood ratio statistic of `r sprintf("%.1f", LR_STAT)` on `r LR_DF`
degrees of freedom and three of four product terms excluding zero. Fitted with inference that
accounts for the clustering of the seedling pattern, every product term spans zero at every block
size tried. The estimates do not move. Only the intervals do, by a factor of
`r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`, and that factor is the entire
distance between a confirmed interaction and no interaction at all.

## Why the third result is the general one {#sec-general}

The parent study's abstract describes the additive effects of increasing beetle to fire disturbance
interactions. Its model has no product term. This paper set out to close that gap by adding one, and
found that the data cannot support a product term either way. That is a more useful outcome than
either of the two the study was designed to produce, because it locates the problem in the inference
rather than in the ecology.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it is not specific to this landscape. A point process
trend fitted by the Berman-Turner device is a weighted Poisson regression [@berman1992; @baddeley2000],
and a Poisson likelihood treats every seedling as an independent piece of evidence about the
covariates. The parent study devotes two figures and fourteen envelope simulations to establishing
that the seedling pattern is not independent: it is clustered at every distance examined, which is
the expected result for conifer regeneration and not a defect [@murphy2026]. Those two facts sit in
the same paper, and the second invalidates the standard errors the first is reported alongside. The
residual correlogram of @tbl-ppcorr reaches the same verdict from inside the model, with dependence
of `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` within 25 m.

This is not an unusual error and it is not a careless one. Clustered point patterns are routinely
fitted this way, and the software makes the Poisson path the path of least resistance. What makes it
consequential here is the size of the correction. A misspecified likelihood does not usually move a
coefficient; it moves the interval around it, and the interval is what the claim rests on. An
interaction reported at p < 10^-16^ and an interaction that cannot be distinguished from zero are the
same number with different error bars.

## What the extent does to both questions {#sec-extent}

Every result here is bounded by an extent chosen by a disturbance rather than by a design. The burn
is about eight square kilometres and the regeneration plots total
`r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha inside it. That is the ground on which beetle and fire co-occur at
all, so it is not an arbitrary choice, but it is not a neutral one either.

The consequences run in the same direction at both scales. Across the burn, lodgepole cover and
elevation correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", R_PL_EL)`, and the two cannot be separated: the companion
study distinguishes them because 1,776 m of relief contains pine-poor ground at every height, and
eight square kilometres does not [@murphy2026refugia]. Inside the burn the fitted elevation optimum
lands at `r round(PEAK)` m, far below the range the clip spans, so an analyst working only here would
report beetle attack rising with elevation without limit. The landscape-scale hump is not
contradicted; it is out of view.

The same collision governs the inference. A block bootstrap needs blocks large enough to contain the
dependence and numerous enough to resample, and at both scales the extent caps the first requirement
before the second is comfortable. Across the burn a 500 m block holds most of the dependence and
affords `r SWEEP$Blocks[SWEEP$"Block side (m)" == BLOCK_M]` blocks; 1 km would afford eight. Inside
the plots the residual range demands 75 to 100 m and the plots afford `r PP_OK_TXT`.
This is the paper's own subject matter arriving in its own
methods: the extent that makes a compound-disturbance question askable is the extent that decides how
firmly it can be answered, and the two pull against each other.

## Limitations {#sec-limits}

**The interaction result is a null, and nulls have a floor.** Nothing here shows that beetle mortality
and burn severity do not interact in their effect on regeneration. It shows that
`r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings across `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha, arranged as
clustered as this pattern is, cannot resolve a difference of differences across four
severity-by-attack combinations. A larger or better distributed sample could return a different
answer, and this study offers no estimate of how much larger.

**Question A is answered in a reduced form.** The within-burn severity gradient is not the question
the compound-disturbance literature asks, which is whether beetle-killed stands burn differently from
stands that were not attacked. Recovering that comparison means rebuilding the classification over
the unclipped landscape from the Landsat archive, which is a reprocessing task and one that re-treads
the parent study's published methods.

**Two beetle surfaces disagree and only one is documented.** The corrected grey-stage union is
preferred throughout because it is three times denser than the published red-stage surface, observed
throughout the perimeter, and derived by a script that survives [@murphy2026greyfix]. The red-stage
surface is a substitution for a layer, `mpb_red_na.tif`, that is absent from the parent repository and
was searched for without success. Where the two surfaces are used together their agreement is
reported and their disagreement is not smoothed over.

**The severity reference category is inherited, not chosen.** The published specification carries
indicators for high and low severity, so moderate severity is pooled with unburned and unclassified
ground into the reference. That pooled category is `r round(100 * REF_MOD / REF_N)` per cent moderate
severity, which is the class carrying the most beetle attack. The specification is reproduced rather
than repaired, because the object of the exercise was to test the published model rather than to
replace it, but no fire coefficient reported here means quite what its label says.

**The provincial survey is a coarse instrument.** It is used as an independent check on whether ground
outside the perimeter carries beetle attack at all, which is a question it can answer, and not as a
measurement of severity, which it cannot. Its polygons are drawn from an aircraft at a mapping scale
far coarser than 30 m.

## What would settle the open questions {#sec-next}

Three things, in descending order of value against cost.

The interaction test should be repeated where the extent is not the binding constraint. The
requirement is not a bigger fire but a regeneration sample distributed across enough independent
blocks that a product term has something to resolve, which given the dependence range measured here
means a plot network rather than three contiguous plots.

The published point process results should be reported with intervals that respect the clustering.
This is inexpensive: the estimates are unchanged and the machinery is the block bootstrap used here.
It affects which main effects in the parent study's Table 12 survive, and on the evidence of
@tbl-ppblocks the answer is that two of them do.

Recovering question A in its original form requires rebuilding the beetle classification over the
unclipped landscape. That is worth doing only if the Landsat archive is being revisited for other
reasons, and it should not be represented as an extension of this analysis.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

Compound disturbance is described as an interaction far more often than it is tested as one, and the
gap between the description and the test is where this study lives.

Three findings, stated at the confidence the data support.

1. **A provenance result.** The beetle surfaces underlying the parent study stop at the fire
   perimeter, in the source files, before classification. Any comparison of beetle attack across that
   boundary measures the clip and not the forest. This is checkable in any study that inherits
   rasters it did not build, and it is cheap to check.

2. **A narrow ecological result.** Inside the burn, beetle attack is elevated at moderate severity
   relative to low, by `r sprintf("%.3f", MOD_ADJ)` in log-odds after conditioning on host and
   elevation, and it clears a spatial block bootstrap interval at every block size the extent
   supports. Attack at high severity is not distinguishable from attack at low severity in any
   specification.

3. **A negative result about the interaction, and a positive one about why.** The beetle by fire
   product term is decisive under the published Poisson likelihood and absent under inference that
   accounts for the clustering the parent study itself documents. The coefficients are identical
   either way. Only the intervals differ, and they differ by a factor of
   `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`.

The title of this paper is a description of the parent study and, on this evidence, a recommendation.
Beetle and fire were modelled additively there. Nothing found here supports modelling them any other
way with data of this extent, and the apparent support for doing so came from a likelihood that
counted clustered seedlings as independent observations. The honest summary of a compound-disturbance
interaction in this landscape is that it has not been demonstrated, that these data cannot
demonstrate it, and that the confidence with which it can appear to have been demonstrated is the
finding most worth carrying elsewhere.
